Is this normal and does anyone have an idea or is the solution as simple as using e.g. 'X2*_df' or 'X2*'?

messages.subject_clean: itemfit sensitive regarding number of respondents?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Janine,

Yes, this is normal and expected behaviour with goodness-of-fit statistics. The bases for these and other measures is to test for *exact* fit, which in reality is extremely unlikely to be strictly true, so increasing sample size may trivially trigger significance tests even though the discrepancy is minor. Looking at ratios such as χ2 / df​​ may be helpful, though these are really just rules of thumb. Also, inspecting the pattern of the residuals will be helpful here too (statistics like S-X2 can compute tables, and there are some other two-step graphical procedures that mirt supports which may provide reasonable approximations of the functional forms). HTH.

Phil

Categorical response data do not have unique residual terms (unlike linear regression models with continuous random variables, they are fully determined by the model expected values). This also means that there's no such thing as a 'residual covariance' parameter as well, though you can make similar specifications by realising that residual correlations are equivalent to having a new latent trait that uniquely loads on the variables that appear to correlate (think a much larger bifactor model).

It isn't, for reasons stated above. Likely the 1*2*3 etc are just ignored because there's no associated factor to match.

messages.subject: Re: M2 (residmat) vs residuals-method
messages.subject_clean: M2 (residmat) vs residuals-method
messages.body_plain:
M2's residuals are based on the linear relationship (in the form of covariance estimates) between the items and how this covariance pattern is "explained" by the IRT model. As such, items must be ordinal by nature in order for this matrix to be of any interpretation use.

The residuals() function returns statistics that are based on the expected values without assuming that covariance is the term which should be explained, but rather the tables of counts directly; hence, LD and such will work with nomial or otherwise non-ordered IRT models. Q3 is a historical statistic really, based on two-step estimates, and probably isn't as optimal in shorter tests. messages.body_plain:
It's possible that some settings have changed across major version iterations, but I think the issue here may have been of over-interpretation of the initial solution. The nominal response model is extremely flexible, and as such tends to have rather high-sampling variability of the estimates. What that means is that, depending on when the model terminates in the estimation, the point estimates may be very different near the ML location, and yet give similar log-likelihood values. Hence, the shape of the curves, when considering this sampling variability, may differ wildly simply due to the likelihood of the parameter range.

With 9 nominal response categories, the SEs would be rather large, and so the certainty of where the true parameter values are is largely a mystery (you'd need extremely large sample sizes to reduce the SE of these kinds of models, 10000+ likely). This is why the nominal model is generally "exploratory", since it gives a general idea of what the IRT function should look like, but the exact shape is too difficult for it to capture due to it's over-flexibility and large sampling variability. HTH.

Phil

> > > Am Dienstag, 30. Januar 2018 18:16:13 UTC+1 schrieb Phil Chalmers:
> > > > M2's residuals are based on the linear relationship (in the form of covariance estimates) between the items and how this covariance pattern is "explained" by the IRT model. As such, items must be ordinal by nature in order for this matrix to be of any interpretation use.
> > > >
> > > > The residuals() function returns statistics that are based on the expected values without assuming that covariance is the term which should be explained, but rather the tables of counts directly; hence, LD and such will work with nomial or otherwise non-ordered IRT models. Q3 is a historical statistic really, based on two-step estimates, and probably isn't as optimal in shorter tests. Overall though, they all have generally the same purpose, though residuals() will return p-value estimates while M2() simply gives the residual covariances values.
